The reviewer is describing a bonus mini-game inside the slot machine experience, apparently a genie-themed wheel. Mechanically, the player watches the wheel land on a large prize, then the genie moves the wheel to a 'spin' outcome and the credited prize ends up far smaller than what was first shown. The reviewer wants the choice to keep the first result instead of being forced to spin on. This describes the game overriding a visibly displayed reward with a lower actual payout - the presentation of the outcome diverges from the settlement of the outcome. No real-money purchase, wager, ad, timer, or social mechanic is mentioned, so monetary, temporal, and social labels are not supported by the text.

labels.label: P_IllusionOfControl
labels.span: in multiple times whe the wheel spin after stopping on a great price the genie move the wheel to a spin tag, and then the prices after the spin are way lower than the original price, from 100 million with 5x multiplier to a 48 million
labels.rationale: The wheel visibly settles on a 500-million-equivalent result and the game then overrides it to a much smaller payout, so the span asserts that the shown outcome is not the real outcome - concealed manipulation of the result rather than a mere unlucky run.

The review complains that the game consumes the player's time. First, a 30-second wait to connect to a match: this is matchmaking/queue latency, a service-side wait rather than a designed timer gate, so Playing by Appointment does not apply. Second, the claim that the game appears to give many rewards but they are 'just for show': this evaluates the reward's worthlessness rather than describing how rewards are delivered, so Reward Mania does not apply. Third, difficulty obtaining weapon upgrades and perks, requiring the player to keep battling: this names the repeated activity (matches/battling) as the route to progression items and frames the time spent as stolen, which matches the repetitive-task-for-progress structure of Grinding. The closing 'rob you of your time' is an evaluation that supports the time-investment reading rather than adding a separate mechanic.

labels.label: T_Grinding
labels.span: Its difficult to get weapon upgrades or any percs others you stick battling to win
labels.rationale: The span names the activity the player must persist in (battling matches) as the way to earn weapon upgrades/perks and win, describing time invested in repeated play rather than skill, which the reviewer then frames as being robbed of time.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer is describing two things about Clash Royale's endgame ladder. First, at high trophy counts (8k+) the opponents they are matched against all use the same handful of overpowered cards (mega knight, pekka, golem), and the reviewer complains that these are frustrating to defend against — this is a card-balance complaint set inside the PvP ladder the game pairs them into. Second, and explicitly repeated twice, the game is 'pay to win': skill alone is said to be insufficient to climb higher, implying that spending money buys an advantage in progression, and the reviewer claims updates keep pushing the game in that direction. Complaints about specific buffs to disliked cards and about having to play 'annoying' strategies are balance and metagame evaluations, not dark-pattern mechanics. Nothing here involves timers, grinding, ads, collections, chance mechanics, or UI manipulation.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: its also pay to win and usually doesn't let you get higher from just using skill
labels.rationale: The reviewer states that money buys an advantage in the game's progression ladder and that skill alone will not get the player higher, which is the paid-advantage instance of the pattern.

labels.label: S_Competition
labels.span: all you play against after 8k trophies is mega knight, pekka, and golem
labels.rationale: The span describes the player being matched against other players on the trophy ladder, so the complaint is about the competitive PvP setting the game places the player in.

parsed.analysis: The review has three components. First, a customer-service complaint about 9 diamonds not being reimbursed: this describes an interaction with support, not a game design rule, so no label arises from it. Second, two statements about spending: the reviewer asserts flatly that one does not have to pay to win (a negation of Pay to Progress, so no tag), and advises readers not to buy beyond 'the pass'. Fishdom's pass is a seasonal paid game pass, which is the named battle-pass indicator of Recurring Fee. Third, the closing advice to get friends and a team and trade lives describes the game's social resource-transfer system, in which players exchange lives with one another, which is Reciprocity.

labels.label: M_RecurringFee
labels.span: you don't buy from this game beyond the pass
labels.rationale: The reviewer references Fishdom's pass as an existing purchasable seasonal item to be bought, which is the battle-pass instance of the recurring fee pattern.

labels.label: S_Reciprocity
labels.span: trade lives
labels.rationale: Trading lives names the resource-transfer system between players, the favour/donation mechanic the definition describes.

parsed.search_query: Fishdom game "pass" season pass what does it include
parsed.search_result: Fishdom's 'pass' refers to its seasonal game pass that players can purchase, providing in-game rewards over a season.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer enjoys the game but makes three suggestions, each pointing at an existing design feature. First, wishing a new life took only 5-10 minutes implies lives currently regenerate on a longer in-game timer, a wait the game imposes on play. Second, 'daily prizes' that must be restarted when a day is missed describe a daily login reward calendar with a penalty for missing a day. Third, 'small and unnecessary tasks like celebrating' is too vague to identify a specific mechanic, and the complaint about harder levels is difficulty feedback, not a pattern. The daily prize reset is a standalone reward loss, not a gate on overall progression, so only the daily-reward label applies to it, while the timed life regeneration is a separate Wait to Play instance.

labels.label: T_PlayingByAppointment
labels.span: maybe only 5-10 minutes for a new life
labels.rationale: Wanting a shorter refill time implies a new life is currently obtained by waiting out an in-game timer, which is the life-regeneration instance of Wait to Play; the suggestion targets the length of the timer, not its existence.

labels.label: T_DailyRewards
labels.span: just because you miss a day doesnt mean that you need to start over on your daily prizes
labels.rationale: Daily prizes that reset when a day is missed are a daily login reward with an active penalty for missing a day, which is the definition exactly.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer is describing ads encountered while playing the game. The complaint centers on the ad interface: no close control is offered, tapping anywhere redirects to the app store, and returning leaves the game stuck on the ad screen until the player force-closes the app. This describes an in-game ad experience that is non-dismissable and intercepts the session, which is a design behavior rather than a technical malfunction in the game itself; the reviewer attributes the behavior to the ad presentation, not to a crash or bug.

labels.label: T_Advertisement
labels.span: after seeing the ads, there is no way to close it. No cross mark on the screen , if you try to click anywhere on the screen it takes you to store. If you go back to game it is still stuck in the last sceeen of the ad. You have to kill the game to come out of the ad screen
labels.rationale: The player is compelled to view the ad to completion because there is no way to dismiss it, and any click routes to the store rather than back to play.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress

labels.rationale: The reviewer states that further progress is contingent on making a payment because energy is no longer given freely, which is the Pay Wall instance: the game reaches a point where progress requires payment.

parsed.analysis: The review describes two things about the game as it currently exists. First, there is a content ceiling: after a while there is little left to do, but this is stated as a general assessment without naming repeated tasks or endless expansion, so it does not reach Grinding or Infinite Treadmill. Second, the core loop is energy-gated: running out of energy halts progress entirely and the regeneration timer is long. That is a design rule in which the game's clock dictates when play can resume, so the only codable mechanic is the energy-regeneration wait that blocks advancement. The remainder of the review is a wish list for a console port and more customization, which describes hypothetical features, not current mechanics.

labels.label: T_PlayingByAppointment

The reviewer describes a timed in-game event with a milestone reward ladder: they were three tasks away from a 525-dice reward, ran out of dice (the resource needed to keep playing), saw the event still showed two days remaining, went to sleep, and on logging back in found the event replaced, so the nearly-completed reward was forfeited. The mechanics at work are: an event that runs on the game's own clock rather than the player's, a reward opportunity that expires on that schedule, and the loss of progress toward a partially completed goal when the schedule lapsed. The reviewer's own response is quitting, so there is no pull-back effect of sunk investment operating on them; the complaint is about the reward expiring while they could not act. No payment is described, and the distrust of F2P models is a general attitude, not a described pay wall or currency conversion. No chance-based delivery or variable reward schedule is described; the event ladder is a predictable milestone structure. The core account is that the game's event deadline took away a nearly earned reward, which is the schedule-imposed loss Playing by Appointment covers.

labels.label: T_PlayingByAppointment
labels.span: The latest event I was about to get 525 dice as reward, I had 3 left to go and I ran out of dice, it said 2Days left. Now just logged in after sleeping and the event is now changed.
labels.rule_applied: Boundary rule vs Fear of missing out: 'Where a reward expires on the game's clock and the span describes the schedule or the loss, code Playing by Appointment.'
labels.rationale: The event's clock ('it said 2Days left', 'the event is now changed') expired while the player was unable to act, forfeiting the near-complete 525-dice reward, so play had to happen on the game's schedule rather than the player's.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer is describing several MONOPOLY GO! systems across one season change. First, they describe a referral-style mechanic: the game had been rewarding them for inviting friends and getting them to join through Facebook, and they complain the reward stopped when the new season started — the recruitment incentive is the mechanic being described even as it fails. Second, they mention struggling to obtain dice, a resource-scarcity complaint with no timer, wait, or payment structure described. Third, playing at max bet and getting no shutdowns or bank heists is a report of an unlucky run, with no claim that outcomes are rigged or that near-wins were frequent. Fourth, sticker rewards arriving 'as duplicates all the way' describes the delivery of repeated, unwanted drops from the randomized sticker pool. Fifth, the login failure with an internet connection error is a technical fault, which R11 excludes. No term is obscure enough to require a search.

labels.label: S_ForcedFellowship
labels.span: Suddenly I get no rewards for inviting friends and getting them to join facebook
labels.rationale: The span describes a design in which in-game rewards are attached to recruiting friends to join through Facebook, which is the invite-others-for-rewards instance of Forced Fellowship; the complaint that the reward stopped does not change what the mechanic is.

labels.label: P_RewardMania
labels.span: Stickers are duplicates all the way
labels.rule_applied: vs Reward described only by its value
labels.rationale: The span describes how rewards are delivered — repeated duplicate drops from the random sticker pool — which is the duplicate-drop delivery indicator, rather than a complaint about a reward's size or value.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes a specific UI behaviour in 8 Ball Pool: whenever the game opens or the player enters the 1v1 section, the interface automatically scrolls to and pre-selects the highest-stakes table the player's coin balance can cover. The reviewer explains the design intent: because the high-stakes table is already selected, the player's normal tap lands on a bet they did not deliberately choose, causing accidental mis-clicks that drain their earned coins and push them toward buying coins with real money. This is a default-option deception: the player must notice and manually change the selection to avoid the unintended stake, and the trick is explicitly tied by the reviewer to real-money purchases ('forced to buy real ones'). The mechanic described is interface-driven friction reduction on spending, not grinding, scheduling, social pressure, or chance-based rewards.

labels.label: M_EasyToPurchase
labels.span: it automatically scrolls and selects the highest possible bet table based on your coins. This is a cheap "Dark UX" trick to force accidental mis-clicks so players lose all their hard-earned coins and are forced to buy real ones.
labels.rule_applied: Accidental Purchases / Default To Purchase (Low Barrier)
labels.rationale: Auto-selecting the highest-stakes table as the default makes an unintended stake easy to commit by a normal mis-click, and the reviewer states the purpose of the design is to drain coins so players have to buy currency with real money; the trick is a default-option deception with no protective step between the tap and the loss.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer is describing late-game economy and difficulty in a solitaire game. Two mechanics are actually being described rather than just evaluated. First, the random deal is said to be biased against the player ('the rng is so obviously against you'), which is a claim that the game's chance outcomes are manipulated rather than neutral bad luck. Second, the level economy is described as a drain: at around level 100 each level costs 2200 coins and a win barely refunds that, so free play is a net loss and the reviewer explicitly frames playing without spending real money as 'not rewarding' — implying the paid route is what keeps the game playable or worthwhile. The complaint that rewards need a revamp is about reward value, not reward delivery, so no Reward Mania. No timers, ads, collections, or social mechanics appear.

labels.label: P_IllusionOfControl
labels.span: the rng is so obviously against you it's crazy
labels.rationale: The span asserts that the random outcome generator is biased against the player, which is a claim of concealed manipulation of how results are determined rather than a mere losing run.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: it's not rewarding playing the game without spending actual money.. at around level 100 it costs 2200 but if you win the level you'll barely make that back
labels.rationale: Level entry costs exceed win refunds so the free route is a net drain, and the span contrasts that unrewarding free play with spending real money, implying payment is the path to continued rewarding progress.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes a base-builder they dismiss as a generic grinder, then focuses on event participation: after weeks of play, a non-spending player cannot win events because skill is irrelevant and victory is determined by money instead ('pay to play' / 'pay to win'), citing that a rival spent a huge real-money amount on the last event to win. The recurring events appear to be ranked contests with other players, since the alternative to paying is framed as having 'no opportunity … to win', and the spend is what purchased the win. The complaint is about design that uses repetitive progression and competitive, pay-gated events rather than about technical quality.

labels.label: T_Grinding
labels.span: Same old same old grinder.
labels.rationale: Calling the game a 'grinder' names the repetitive task cycle required to advance, rather than merely the review's mood.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: Zero skill pay to play. Zero skill pay to win. Calculated total spent on last event was 30k to win.

parsed.analysis: The review is a numbered list of complaints about Candy Crush Soda Saga's economy. Complaint 1 says the game 'charged' premium gold pieces for extra moves at a moment when the player still had moves left, describing an unintended or unneeded charge with no sign the player deliberately consented to it — i.e., a purchase that should not have gone through. Complaint 2 says a paid package failed to deliver its advertised lives; that is a delivery/customer-service failure, not a designed dark pattern. Complaint 3 says timed bonuses keep counting down while the app is closed, so the value of the bonuses is lost unless the player plays inside the window the game's clock defines. Complaint 4 states that gold (Candy Crush's premium currency, bought with real money) cannot be earned in sufficient amounts to keep playing without buying, so continued play is contingent on purchasing currency. Complaints 5 and 6 are price and policy opinions: packages cost too much and should not be timed, restating the timer problem already covered. No term needs an external lookup; the review names the mechanics directly.

labels.label: M_EasyToPurchase
labels.span: I was charged 10 gold pcs for 5 moves, I had 2 moves left.
labels.rationale: The player was charged premium currency for moves they did not need while moves remained, so the charge went through without their intended consent, implying no confirmation or undo step stood between them and the purchase.

labels.label: T_PlayingByAppointment
labels.span: The timed bonuses tick away even though I am not playing. I go to bed with bonuses to wake up with them almost gone or gone.
labels.rationale: Timed bonuses run on the game's clock and deplete while the player is away, so the player must play within the window the game defines or forfeit the bonuses.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: You cannot win enough gold to play without buying sometimes.
labels.rationale: Continued play is stated to be contingent on buying gold because winnings fall short, so progress stops unless payment is made.

labels.label: M_IntermediateCurrency
labels.span: You cannot win enough gold to play without buying sometimes.
labels.rationale: Gold is the premium currency that the span says must be bought, so real money is being converted into in-game currency to sustain play.

parsed.analysis: The review is mostly about in-app purchases for an album-completion collectible system. The reviewer is two cards short of completing an album and buying a deal seemingly promising to supply cards; instead of the missing cards they receive duplicates, so they call it a scam. The core mechanics described are: collecting a fixed album set where completion carries a grand prize (collectible/collection drive); purchasable deals that deliver randomly drawn cards so duplicates are possible (chance-based reward delivery with a real-money stake); and I need to clarify that 'cards' here come from Dice Dreams' sticker/album system rather than, say, card game strategy.

labels.label: P_CompleteTheCollection
labels.span: I had two cards left which would grant me the grand prize for completing an album
labels.rationale: The player is only two cards away from a complete album and frames that missing-card state as the motivation for the purchase, so the collection drive is what the text describes.

labels.label: M_Gambling
labels.span: i bought a deal which promised i would get NEW cards, and all i got were useless duplicates!
labels.rationale: The purchase is a real-money stake, and the outcome is not fixed: the deal is said to promise new cards but the player still receives duplicates, so the cards appear delivered by a chance-based draw rather than a guaranteed item.

labels.label: P_RewardMania
labels.span: all i got were useless duplicates!
labels.rationale: The deal draws from a random card pool, and receiving duplicates shows the delivery is unpredictable and repeated rather than based on the reward's value, which is the variable-reward delivery mechanism.

parsed.search_query: Dice Dreams sticker album deal buying cards duplicates new cards
parsed.search_result: Dice Dreams' 'cards' are collectible album stickers, and purchases/deals deliver cards that can duplicate; players seek missing stickers to complete albums for a grand prize.

parsed.analysis: The review makes three distinct claims about the game as it currently is. First, that patch rewards have shrunk over time; that is a complaint about the size of rewards, not about how rewards are delivered, so on its own it does not reach Reward Mania. Second, that the meta is constantly shifting and the player must pull new characters to deal damage; this describes the value of the player's existing characters eroding as the meta moves, which is Power Creep, and it names the gacha pull mechanic as the required channel. Third, that the game is becoming 'pay 2 win', which asserts that spending money confers the combat advantage needed. The closing remark about a low-quality background image in a quest is an aesthetic/quality complaint with no design mechanic behind it. The terms used (archon quest, Mavuika, Natlan, pulls, meta) are standard Genshin vocabulary and need no external lookup.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: the game is getting more and more pay 2 win
labels.rationale: The reviewer explicitly states the game increasingly gives advantages to players who spend, which is the Pay to Win instance of Pay to Progress.

labels.label: M_PowerCreep
labels.span: the Meta changes more and more every single day basically forcing us to pull for new characters if we want to actually do damage
labels.rationale: Rapid meta shifts mean the characters the player already owns stop being able to deal damage, so acquired value diminishes and new purchases are pushed, which is Power Creep.

labels.label: P_RewardMania
labels.span: forcing us to pull for new characters
labels.rule_applied: Gacha mechanics like pulls, rolls, banners
labels.rationale: Pulling names Genshin's gacha wishing system, a chance-based character delivery mechanic, and no monetary stake for the pulls is explicitly described, so Reward Mania applies without Gambling.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes two in-game realities after dismissing the game's marketing. First, the game is 'a base growth simulator teeming with micro transaction menus' - the latter is only a statement about the volume of purchase offers, with no mechanism such as default-to-purchase, small close buttons, or misdirection described, so no Monetary label attaches to it. Second, the reviewer describes endgame PvP: 'players are encouraged to attack each other' - that is the game putting players into competition with one another, which is Competition. Third, the 'huge gap between p2w and f2p' names the paid and free player classes and asserts a divide between them, implying that spending money confers an advantage in that competition, which is the Pay to Win instance of Pay to Progress. The 'nothing like what's advertised' complaint concerns out-of-game marketing and is excluded from coding.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: there's a huge gap between p2w and f2p
labels.rule_applied: Pay to Win (low-level indicator); vs Free alternative boundary
labels.rationale: Naming the pay-to-win and free-to-play classes and the gap between them implies that players who spend money hold an advantage over those who do not, which is the Pay to Win instance.

labels.label: S_Competition
labels.span: players are encouraged to attack each other
labels.rationale: The design pushes players into attacking one another, which is the game making players compete against each other.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer is describing the current state of the game after an update. Two design behaviours come through. First, growth is gated behind payment: 'You have to spend to have any meaningful growth' states that meaningful progression is contingent on spending money, with no free path described — a Pay Wall. Second, the update removed 'open silver' and any player-vs-player play, which the reviewer says made the paid-for growth pointless and 'screwed over' those who spent money; that is an update devaluing purchases players already made, matching how Power Creep treats rebalancing/updates that strip value from acquired investments. The PvP element itself is described only as having been removed, so it is not a currently present mechanic and cannot be coded as Competition under R12. 'Boring farmville' and 'Save your time and money' are evaluations and advice, not mechanics. The term 'open silver' is a removed feature and no label depends on identifying it, so no search is needed.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: You have to spend to have any meaningful growth
labels.rationale: Meaningful progress is stated to be contingent on spending money, with no free alternative described, which is the Pay Wall instance of Pay to Progress.

labels.label: M_PowerCreep

labels.rule_applied: definition (value of paid items diminished over time through updates)
labels.rationale: The update removed the game mode that gave paid-for growth its value, so purchases made earlier lose value after acquisition through an update, the devaluation Power Creep describes.
